vsm1.6:70.1: The livid should be brought to mind as “Repulsiveness of the livid, repulsiveness of the livid.”
vsm1.6:70.2: Here the learning sign appears blotchy-coloured;
vsm1.6:70.3: but the counterpart sign’s appearance has the colour which is most prevalent.
vsm1.6:71.1: The festering should be brought to mind as “Repulsiveness of the festering, repulsiveness of the festering.”
vsm1.6:71.2: Here the learning sign appears as though trickling;
vsm1.6:71.3: but the counterpart sign appears motionless and quiet.
vsm1.6:72.1: The cut up is found on a battlefield or in a robbers’ forest or on a charnel ground where kings have robbers cut up
vsm1.6:72.2: or in the jungle in a place where men are torn up by lions and tigers.
vsm1.6:72.3: So, if when he goes there, it comes into focus at one adverting although lying in different places, that is good.
vsm1.6:72.4: If not, then he should not touch it with his own hand;
vsm1.6:72.5: for by doing so he would become familiar with it.
vsm1.6:72.6: He should get a monastery attendant or one studying to become an ascetic or someone else to put it together in one place.
vsm1.6:72.7: If he cannot find anyone to do it,
vsm1.6:72.8: he should put it together with a walking stick or a staff in such a way that there is only a finger’s breadth separating the parts.
vsm1.6:72.9: Having put it together thus, he should bring it to mind as “Repulsiveness of the cut up, repulsiveness of the cut up.”
vsm1.6:72.10: Herein, the learning sign appears as though cut in the middle;
vsm1.6:72.11: but the counterpart sign appears whole.
vsm1.6:73.1: The gnawed should be brought to mind as “Repulsiveness of the gnawed, repulsiveness of the gnawed.”
vsm1.6:73.2: Here the learning sign appears as though gnawed here and there;
vsm1.6:73.3: but the counterpart sign appears whole.
vsm1.6:74.1:
After getting the scattered put together or putting it together in the way described under
the cut up so that there is only a finger’s breadth, separating the pieces,
vsm1.6:74.2: it should be brought to mind as “Repulsiveness of the scattered, repulsiveness of the scattered.”
vsm1.6:74.3: Here the learning sign appears with the gaps evident;
vsm1.6:74.4: but the counterpart sign appears whole.
vsm1.6:75.1: The hacked and scattered is found in the same places as those described under the cut up.
vsm1.6:75.2:
Therefore, after going there and getting it put together or putting it together in the way described
under the cut up so that there is only a finger’s breadth separating the pieces,
vsm1.6:75.3: it should be brought to mind as “Repulsiveness of the hacked and scattered, repulsiveness of the hacked and scattered.”
vsm1.6:75.4: Here, when the learning sign becomes evident, it does so with the fissures of the wounds;
vsm1.6:75.5: but the counterpart sign appears whole.
vsm1.6:76.1:
The bleeding is found at the time when blood is trickling from the openings of wounds received on battlefields,
etc., or from the openings of burst boils and abscesses when the hands and feet have been cut off.
vsm1.6:76.2: So on seeing that, it should be brought to mind as “Repulsiveness of the bleeding, repulsiveness of the bleeding.”
vsm1.6:76.3: Here the learning sign appears to have the aspect of moving like a red banner struck by wind;
vsm1.6:76.4: but the counterpart sign appears quiet.
vsm1.6:77.1: There is a worm-infested corpse when at the end of two or three days a mass of maggots oozes out from the corpse’s nine orifices,
vsm1.6:77.2:
and the mass lies there like a heap of paddy or boiled rice as big as the body, whether the body is that of a dog,
a jackal, a human being, an ox, a buffalo, an elephant, a horse, a python, or what you will.
vsm1.6:77.3:
It can be brought to mind with respect to anyone of these as “Repulsiveness of the worm-infested,
repulsiveness of the worm-infested.”
vsm1.6:77.4: For the sign arose for the Elder Cūḷa-Piṇḍapātika-Tissa in the corpse of an elephant’s carcass in the Kāḷadīghavāpi reservoir.
vsm1.6:77.5: Here the learning sign appears as though moving;
vsm1.6:77.6: but the counterpart sign appears quiet, like a ball of boiled rice.
vsm1.6:78.1:
A skeleton is described in various aspects in the way beginning “As though he were looking at a corpse thrown
onto a charnel ground, a skeleton with flesh and blood, held together by sinews” (D II 296).
vsm1.6:78.2: So he should go in the way already described to where it has been put,
vsm1.6:78.3: and noticing any stones, etc., with their surrounding signs and in relation, to the object,
vsm1.6:78.4: he should characterize it by the fact of its having attained that particular individual essence thus, “This is a skeleton,”
vsm1.6:78.5: and he should apprehend the sign in the eleven ways by colour and the rest.
vsm1.6:78.6:
But if he looks at it, apprehending it only by its colour as white, it does
not appear to him with its individual essence as repulsive,
vsm1.6:78.7: but only as a variant of the white kasiṇa.
vsm1.6:78.8: Consequently he should only look at it as ‘a skeleton’ in the repulsive aspect.
vsm1.6:79.1: “Mark” is a term for the hand, etc., here,
vsm1.6:79.2: so he should define it by its mark according to hand, foot, head, chest, arm, waist, thigh, and shin.
vsm1.6:79.3: He should define it by its shape, however, according as it is long, short, square, round, small or large.
vsm1.6:79.4: By its direction and by its location are as already described (§39–40).
vsm1.6:79.5: Having defined it by its delimitation according to the periphery of each bone,
vsm1.6:79.6: he should reach absorption by apprehending whichever appears most evident to him.
vsm1.6:79.7: But it can also be defined by its concavities and by its convexities according to the concave and convex places in each bone.
vsm1.6:79.8: And it can also be defined by position thus:
vsm1.6:79.9: “I am standing in a concave place, the skeleton is in a convex place;
vsm1.6:79.10: or I am standing in a convex place, the skeleton is in a concave place.”
vsm1.6:79.11: It should be defined by its joints according as any two bones are joined together.
vsm1.6:79.12: It should be defined by its openings according to the gaps separating the bones.
vsm1.6:79.13: It should be defined all round by directing knowledge to it comprehensively thus: “In this place there is this skeleton.”
vsm1.6:79.14: If the sign does not arise even in this way, then the mind should be established on the frontal bone.
vsm1.6:79.16:
just as in the case of those that precede it beginning with the worm-infested,
the apprehending of the sign should be observed in this elevenfold manner as appropriate.
vsm1.6:80.1: This meditation subject is successful with a whole skeleton frame and even with a single bone as well.
vsm1.6:80.2: So having learnt the sign in anyone of these in the eleven ways,
vsm1.6:80.3: he should bring it to mind as “Repulsiveness of a skeleton, repulsiveness of a skeleton.”
vsm1.6:80.4: Here the learning sign and the counterpart sign are alike, so it is said.
vsm1.6:80.5: That is correct for a single bone.
vsm1.6:80.6: But when the learning sign becomes manifest in a skeleton frame, what is correct to say is that there are gaps in the learning sign
vsm1.6:80.7: while the counterpart sign appears whole.
vsm1.6:80.8: And the learning sign even in a single bone should be dreadful and terrifying
vsm1.6:80.9: but the counterpart sign produces happiness and joy because it brings access.
vsm1.6:81.1: What is said in the Commentaries in this context allows that deduction.
vsm1.6:81.2: For there, after saying this, “There is no counterpart sign in the four divine abidings and in the ten kinds of foulness;
vsm1.6:81.3: for in the case of the divine abidings the sign is the breaking down of boundaries itself,
vsm1.6:81.4:
and in the case of the ten kinds of foulness the sign comes into being as soon
as the repulsiveness is seen, without any thinking about it,”
vsm1.6:81.5: it is again said, immediately next:
vsm1.6:81.6: “Here the sign is twofold: the learning sign and the counterpart sign.
vsm1.6:81.7: The learning sign appears hideous, dreadful and terrifying,” and so on.
vsm1.6:81.8: So what we said was well considered.
vsm1.6:81.9: And it is only this that is correct here.
vsm1.6:81.10:
Besides, the appearance of a woman’s whole body as a collection of bones to the Elder Mahā-Tissa
through his merely looking at her teeth demonstrates this here (see I.55).
vsm1.6:82.1:
The Divine Ruler with ten hundred eyes
Did him with the Ten Powers eulogize,
Who, fair in fame, made known as cause of jhāna
This foulness of ten species in such wise.
vsm1.6:82.2:
Now, knowing their description and the way
To tackle each and how they are developed,
There are some further points that will repay
Study, each with its special part to play.
vsm1.6:83.1: One who has reached jhāna in anyone of these
vsm1.6:83.2: goes free from cupidity; he resembles an Arahant without greed because his greed has been well suppressed.
vsm1.6:83.4: this classification of foulness should be understood as stated
vsm1.6:83.5: in accordance with the particular individual essences successively reached by the dead body
vsm1.6:83.6: and also in accordance with the particular subdivisions of the greedy temperament.
vsm1.6:84.1: When a corpse has entered upon the repulsive state,
vsm1.6:84.2: it may have reached the individual essence of the bloated
vsm1.6:84.3: or anyone of the individual essences beginning with that of the livid.
vsm1.6:84.4:
So the sign should be apprehended as “Repulsiveness of the bloated,” “Repulsiveness of the livid,”
according to whichever he has been able to find.
vsm1.6:84.5:
This, it should be understood, is how the classification of foulness comes to be tenfold with the body’s
arrival at each particular individual essence.
vsm1.6:85.1: And individually the bloated suits one who is greedy about shape since it makes evident the disfigurement of the body’s shape.
vsm1.6:85.2: The livid suits one who is greedy about the body’s colour since it makes evident the disfigurement of the skin’s colour.
vsm1.6:85.3:
The festering suits one who is greedy about the smell of the body aroused by scents, perfumes,
etc., since it makes evident the evil smells connected with this sore, the body.
vsm1.6:85.4: The cut up suits one who is greedy about compactness in the body since it makes evident the hollowness inside it.
vsm1.6:85.5:
The gnawed suits one who is greedy about accumulation of flesh in such parts of the body as the breasts
since it makes it evident how a fine accumulation of flesh comes to nothing.
vsm1.6:85.6: The scattered suits one who is greedy about the grace of the limbs since it makes it evident how limbs can be scattered.
vsm1.6:85.7:
The hacked and scattered suits one who is greedy about a fine body as a whole since it makes
evident the disintegration and alteration of the body as a whole.
vsm1.6:85.8:
The bleeding suits one who is greedy about elegance produced by ornaments since it
makes evident its repulsiveness when smeared with blood.
vsm1.6:85.9:
The worm-infested suits one who is greedy about ownership of the body since it makes it
evident how the body is shared with many families of worms.
vsm1.6:85.10: A skeleton suits one who is greedy about fine teeth since it makes evident the repulsiveness of the bones in the body.
vsm1.6:85.11:
This, it should be understood, is how the classification of foulness comes to be tenfold
according to the subdivisions of the greedy temperament.
vsm1.6:86.1: But as regards the tenfold foulness,
vsm1.6:86.2: just as it is only by virtue of its rudder that a boat keeps steady in a river with turbulent waters and a rapid current,
vsm1.6:86.3: and it cannot be steadied without a rudder,
vsm1.6:86.4: so too here, owing to the weak hold on the object, consciousness when unified only keeps steady by virtue of applied thought,
vsm1.6:86.5: and it cannot be steadied without applied thought,
vsm1.6:86.6: which is why there is only the first jhāna here, not the second and the rest.
vsm1.6:87.1: And repulsive as this object is,
vsm1.6:87.2:
still it arouses joy and happiness in him by his seeing its advantages thus,
“Surely in this way I shall be liberated from ageing and death,”
vsm1.6:87.3: and by his abandoning the hindrances’ oppression;
vsm1.6:87.4: just as a garbage heap does in a flower-scavenger by his seeing the advantages thus, “Now I shall get a high wage,”
vsm1.6:87.5: and as the workings of purges and emetics do in a man suffering the pains of sickness.
vsm1.6:88.1: This foulness, while of ten kinds, has only one characteristic.
vsm1.6:88.2:
For though it is of ten kinds, nevertheless its characteristic is only its impure,
stinking, disgusting and repulsive state (essence).
vsm1.6:88.3: And foulness appears with this characteristic not only in a dead body
vsm1.6:88.4: but also in a living one, as it did to the Elder Mahā-Tissa who lived at Cetiyapabbata (I.55),
vsm1.6:88.5: and to the novice attendant on the Elder Saṅgharakkhita while he was watching the king riding an elephant.
vsm1.6:88.6: For a living body is just as foul as a dead one,
vsm1.6:88.7: only the characteristic of foulness is not evident in a living body, being hidden by adventitious embellishments.
vsm1.6:89.1: This is the body’s nature: it is a collection of over three hundred bones, jointed by one hundred and eighty joints,
vsm1.6:89.2: bound together by nine hundred sinews, plastered over with nine hundred pieces of flesh,
vsm1.6:89.3: enveloped in the moist inner skin, enclosed in the outer cuticle, with orifices here and there,
vsm1.6:89.4: constantly dribbling and trickling like a grease pot, inhabited by a community of worms,
vsm1.6:89.5: the home of disease, the basis of painful states,
vsm1.6:89.6: perpetually oozing from the nine orifices like a chronic open carbuncle,
vsm1.6:89.7: from both of whose eyes eye-filth trickles, from whose ears comes ear-filth,
vsm1.6:89.8: from whose nostrils snot, from whose mouth food and bile and phlegm and blood,
vsm1.6:89.9: from whose lower outlets excrement and urine, and from whose ninety-nine thousand pores the broth of stale sweat seeps,
vsm1.6:89.10: with bluebottles and their like buzzing round it,
vsm1.6:89.11: which when untended with tooth sticks and mouth-washing and head-anointing and bathing and underclothing and dressing would,
vsm1.6:89.12:
judged by the universal repulsiveness of the body, make even a king, if he wandered from village to village with his hair
in its natural wild disorder, no different from a flower-scavenger or an outcaste or what you will.
vsm1.6:89.13:
So there is no distinction between a king’s body and an outcaste’s in so far
as its impure stinking nauseating repulsiveness is concerned.
vsm1.6:90.1: But by rubbing out the stains on its teeth with tooth sticks and mouth-washing and all that,
vsm1.6:90.2: by concealing its private parts under several cloths,
vsm1.6:90.3: by daubing it with various scents and salves,
vsm1.6:90.4: by pranking it with nosegays and such things,
vsm1.6:90.5: it is worked up into a state that permits of its being taken as “I” and “mine.”
vsm1.6:90.6:
So men delight in women and women in men without perceiving the true nature of its characteristic
foulness, now masked by this adventitious adornment.
vsm1.6:90.7: But in the ultimate sense there is no place here even the size of an atom fit to lust after.
vsm1.6:91.1:
And then, when any such bits of it as head hairs, body hairs, nails, teeth, spittle,
snot, excrement or urine have dropped off the body,
vsm1.6:91.3: they are ashamed, humiliated and disgusted.
vsm1.6:91.4: But as long as anyone of these things remains in it,
vsm1.6:91.5: though it is just as repulsive,
vsm1.6:91.6:
they take it as agreeable, desirable, permanent, pleasant, self, because they
are wrapped in the murk of ignorance and dyed with affection and greed for self.
vsm1.6:91.8:
they resemble the old jackal who saw a flower not yet fallen from a kiṃsuka tree in a forest and yearned
after it, thinking, “This is a piece of meat, it is a piece of meat.”
vsm1.6:92.1:
There was a jackal chanced to see
A flowering kiṃsuka in a wood;
In haste he went to where it stood:
“I have found a meat-bearing tree!”
vsm1.6:92.2:
He chewed the blooms that fell, but could,
Of course, find nothing fit to eat;
He took it thus: “Unlike the meat
There on the tree, this is no good.”
vsm1.6:92.3:
A wise man will not think to treat
As foul only the part that fell,
But treats as foul the part as well
That in the body has its seat.
vsm1.6:92.4:
Fools cannot in their folly tell;
They take the body to be fair,
And soon get caught in Evil’s snare
Nor can escape its painful spell.
vsm1.6:92.5:
But since the wise have thus laid bare
This filthy body’s nature, so,
Be it alive or dead, they know
There is no beauty lurking there.
vsm1.6:93.2:
“This filthy body stinks outright
Like ordure, like a privy’s site;
This body men that have insight
Condemn, as object of a fool’s delight.
vsm1.6:93.3:
“A tumour where nine holes abide
Wrapped in a coat of clammy hide
And trickling filth on every side,
Polluting the air with stenches far and wide.
vsm1.6:93.4:
“If it perchance should come about
That what is inside it came out,
Surely a man would need a knout
With which to put the crows and dogs to rout.”
vsm1.6:94.1:
So a capable bhikkhu should apprehend the sign wherever the aspect of foulness is manifest,
whether in a living body or in a dead one,
vsm1.6:94.2: and he should make the meditation subject reach absorption.
vsm1.6:94.3:
The sixth chapter called “The Description of Foulness as
a Meditation Subject” in the Treatise on the Development
of Concentration in the Path of Purification composed for
the purpose of gladdening good people.
